narrative:
The model estimates a 37% chance that you will not pass your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. Among students who passed, the average number of prior failures is zero, so this history pulled the prediction strongly toward failing. Your weekly study time of 5–10 hours was the second most important influence; although this amount is not unusually low, the model sees it as less than the typical study habits of students who ultimately succeed, nudging the outcome slightly toward failure. Finally, the fact that you do want to pursue higher education worked in your favor and pushed the prediction back toward passing, but not enough to outweigh the other two factors.

To improve, focus first on breaking the pattern of past failures by seeking help early in every subject. Consider increasing your weekly study time beyond 5–10 hours and using that time more effectively, perhaps with structured support. Because you already aspire to continue studying after school, turning that motivation into consistent daily effort can shift your trajectory. Taking the remedial courses seriously is a practical next step to close the gaps the model has highlighted.
